Original Transcript: page five    It had "been concluded by now that it was dangerous to try  further to prepare the administrations for what was coming. For  one thing the paid informers talked often to others than SLED.  By now, the professors themselves operated contacts which kept  their faction informed. It was unfortunate that this was the  case because there was still opportunity to defeat the campaign  against the colleges - and no matter how it is otherwise stated,  those making the attack had no concern over the probable damage  being done to the colleges themselves.    There are two developments along this line I report.    First, the actual discreditation of graduates in teaching  at Allen was never planned. What happened was that a scheme  was decided on, under which a letter threatening discreditation  was to be sent to AllenΓÇÖs administration which could in private  be used as compulsion for the dismissals sought at that college.  It was expressly understood that the letter was never to have  been made public, for the proposed action would likely provoke  reactions dangerous to the personal program of the Governor.    However, by an unusual development, contents of the letter  became public information even before it reached its intended  source at Allen. This infuriated Gov. Timmerman who left office  still uncertain as to how or where the leak came. He both  accused Allen of breaking its word, and at the same time, fired  his office aide, Charles Wickenberg - then a former reporter -  whom he suspected of leaking the matter to former co-workers.  Actually, Mr. Wickenberg was innocent.    Gov. Timmerman was now backed into a corner. If Allen didnΓÇÖt  dismiss its professors the threat of the mandate had to be obeyed.  For certain reasons, Allen demurred again on firing the three men  in question. Finally, the discreditation came and continued  until the men were relieved of their positions.    Since the spring of 19%, the GovernorΓÇÖs office had also had  assistance and cooperation from a white source which, for years,  had been considered influential with certain Negroes. This white  man, a lawyer, was placed on the Trustee Board of South Carolina  State College when a Board member from Sumter county died in the  spring of 19%. The manΓÇÖs firm had represented Allen University  for many years. He was also most influential with two Negro  members of the Benedict College Trustee Board. It appears that  we used both of his connections to the benefit of the Governor  in the Columbia disputes.    Once the Allen dismissals neared attainment, great pressures  were applied on certain Benedict Trustees, who in turn made certain  representations upon its President who, as pointed out earlier,  had irritated the Governor in refusing to play ball. Details of  this maneuver, of how both white and colored trustees were  bludgeoned - largely by the white attorney - into forcing the  dismissals at Benedict is both interesting and unique.

Original Transcript: FOREWORD    Most universities have a tower. Tall or massive, soaring  or brooding, graceful or ungainly, it presides over the campus  as the symbol of a seat of learning.    Tradition could inspire no better symbol for the  University. A tower is a place to see in every direction be┬¼  hind and ahead. It beckons the wanderer and guides the  uncertain. Our tower is the clock which has been repainted  and partially repaired. Anchored solidly, it has an upward  thrust that calls with inspiration and promise.    In Allen University man has created--ln fact the African  Methodist Episcopal Church has created--his mechanism for pre┬¼  serving and understanding his Christian heritage in order to  serve his present and future needs. It has delivered to each  generation the steadily growing heritage of the past. On this  foundation each generation has built, imperfectly, yet often  well.    It is proper for each generationΓÇöand this one perhaps  more than any otherΓÇöto inquire into its university, to test  its excellence, to question its progress, and to search its  motive. No less does the University deserve the thoughtful  attention of society, for its cause is ultimately the cause  of man, neglected or taken for granted at his peril.

I have also checked  back over other matters you mentioned and, especially,  into the background of the AAUP situation with emphasis on  what precipitated it.    I thought to write you this personal letter so that  in the future you may be enabled to understand my pro┬¼  fessional role more clearly and spared the factor of  suspicion and distrust - if you wish it that way. IΓÇÖm presuming that the writer maXEhEdxfants simply  did thd logical thing: meld facts from the AUUP action in  Chicago with other documented and wellknown facts, which  involved both Allen and Benedict College, and also the  GovernorΓÇÖs office. I do not detect anywhere the slightest  basis for suspecting that the reporter writing the story  may have slanted his account to the benefit of either  college, or went beyond normal limits in reporting on a  situation which affected and involved both of the colleges.    In following this procedure the reporter employed the  same kind of freedom in his or her profession which seems  to be the substance of the AAUPΓÇÖs position in its censures  of both Allen and Benedict. Moreover, the two colleges are  inseparably connected in the issue of the dismissed pro┬¼  fessors; to the extent even that both colleges employed the  services of most or all of these persons in a joint faculty  operation program for some classes. Both colleges were put  under pressure by the State, for the same reasons, and both  colleges dismissed the men - perhaps, reluctantly and regret┬¼  fully at the time. Both were subsequently hauled onto the  AAUP carpet.    I setforth all of this that you might understand how  BenedictΓÇÖs name got intxb the story.    For some time I have been wanting to evaluate this  entire matter. I have never written this story,  and perhaps never will - for publication, but oddly, it all"  began with Benedict College, a fact you may rnnii recall.

Original Transcript: page five    It had "been concluded by now that it was dangerous to try  further to prepare the administrations for what was coming. For  one thing the paid informers talked often to others than SLED.  By now, the professors themselves operated contacts which kept  their faction informed. It was unfortunate that this was the  case because there was still opportunity to defeat the campaign  against the colleges - and no matter how it is otherwise stated,  those making the attack had no concern over the probable damage  being done to the colleges themselves.    There are two developments along this line I report.    First, the actual discreditation of graduates in teaching  at Allen was never planned. What happened was that a scheme  was decided on, under which a letter threatening discreditation  was to be sent to AllenΓÇÖs administration which could in private  be used as compulsion for the dismissals sought at that college.  It was expressly understood that the letter was never to have  been made public, for the proposed action would likely provoke  reactions dangerous to the personal program of the Governor.    However, by an unusual development, contents of the letter  became public information even before it reached its intended  source at Allen. This infuriated Gov. Timmerman who left office  still uncertain as to how or where the leak came. He both  accused Allen of breaking its word, and at the same time, fired  his office aide, Charles Wickenberg - then a former reporter -  whom he suspected of leaking the matter to former co-workers.  Actually, Mr. Wickenberg was innocent.    Gov. Timmerman was now backed into a corner. If Allen didnΓÇÖt  dismiss its professors the threat of the mandate had to be obeyed.  For certain reasons, Allen demurred again on firing the three men  in question. Finally, the discreditation came and continued  until the men were relieved of their positions.    Since the spring of 19%, the GovernorΓÇÖs office had also had  assistance and cooperation from a white source which, for years,  had been considered influential with certain Negroes. This white  man, a lawyer, was placed on the Trustee Board of South Carolina  State College when a Board member from Sumter county died in the  spring of 19%. The manΓÇÖs firm had represented Allen University  for many years. He was also most influential with two Negro  members of the Benedict College Trustee Board. It appears that  we used both of his connections to the benefit of the Governor  in the Columbia disputes.    Once the Allen dismissals neared attainment, great pressures  were applied on certain Benedict Trustees, who in turn made certain  representations upon its President who, as pointed out earlier,  had irritated the Governor in refusing to play ball. Details of  this maneuver, of how both white and colored trustees were  bludgeoned - largely by the white attorney - into forcing the  dismissals at Benedict is both interesting and unique.

Original Transcript: FOREWORD    Most universities have a tower. Tall or massive, soaring  or brooding, graceful or ungainly, it presides over the campus  as the symbol of a seat of learning.    Tradition could inspire no better symbol for the  University. A tower is a place to see in every direction be┬¼  hind and ahead. It beckons the wanderer and guides the  uncertain. Our tower is the clock which has been repainted  and partially repaired. Anchored solidly, it has an upward  thrust that calls with inspiration and promise.    In Allen University man has created--ln fact the African  Methodist Episcopal Church has created--his mechanism for pre┬¼  serving and understanding his Christian heritage in order to  serve his present and future needs. It has delivered to each  generation the steadily growing heritage of the past. On this  foundation each generation has built, imperfectly, yet often  well.    It is proper for each generationΓÇöand this one perhaps  more than any otherΓÇöto inquire into its university, to test  its excellence, to question its progress, and to search its  motive. Original Transcript: TRUE THEN    and  TRUE NOW...    TEN THINGS YOU CANNOT DO...    1. You cannot bring about prosperity  by discouraging thrift.    2. You cannot strengthen the weak  by weakening the strong.    3. You cannot help strong men by  tearing down big men.    4. You cannot help the wage earner  by pulling down the wage payer.    5. You cannot further the brotherhood of man by encouraging class  hatred.    6. You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich.    7. You cannot establish sound security  on borrowed money.    8. You cannot keep out of trouble  by spending more than you earn.    9. You cannot build character and  courage by taking away man's initiative and independence.    10. You cannot help men permanently  by doing for them what they could  and should do for themselves.    ΓÇöAbraham Lincoln    A Timely Thought ...    Labor "Leaders" are again talking shorter  and shorter work weeksΓÇö35 and even 30 hours  per week. Why not 20 or 10? How about a full  day's work each Monday, then everybody enjoy  a six day week-end?    But who would raise the food, and make the  clothing, and refine the gasoline everyone would  need to ENJOY his six day week-end?    In spite of the rabble rousers every intelligent  workman knows he can be paid only out of what  he produces and if he wants more leisure time    he must produce that much more in the reduced  time he works. It is just that simple.    That is what modern machines are forΓÇöto  help him do exactly that. (Or work the same  hours and produce more so that he can be paid  more.)    All the talk in the world cannot change this  fact. You cannot DIVIDE what isn't first  PRODUCED. The better you use your machines  and your time to produce more efficiently the  more there will be for you to divide, more honest  leisure, more pay, and more self respect.
